newsitem.title: ITALY: Tennis-Australia's Draper downs Muster in Rome heat.
newsitem.headline: Tennis-Australia's Draper downs Muster in Rome heat.

text.p: Defending champion Thomas Muster saw his dream of a third successive Italian Open title die in the heat of a three-hour battle with unseeded Australian Scott Draper at the Foro Italico on Wednesday.

The third seed, unbeaten in Rome since the third round in 1994 and three times a winner, received treatment for dehydration after losing his second round match 7-6 5-7 7-5 in temperatures of 32 degrees Celsius.
The Austrian failed to turn up for a post match news conference after the tournament doctor sent him to his hotel with orders to rest.
"Muster's game is very demanding," said Boris Becker, who beat France's Cedric Pioline 6-4 7-5. "One hundred and fifty times his opponents wind up like he did."
Muster's exit left the tournament without four of its top five seeds after two rounds for the first time.
Reigning Wimbledon champion and fifth seed Richard Krajicek joined the list of big-name casualties when he surrendered 7-6 7-6 to German Marc-Kevin Goellner.
The world's top two players, Pete Sampras and Michael Chang, lost in the first round on Tuesday.
At one stage it looked as if French Open champion Yvegeny Kafelnikov might add his name to the list as Dutchman Paul Haarhuis pushed their match into a final set.
But the Russian fourth seed survived 7-6 3-6 6-3 and will play Spain's Alberto Berasategui for a quarter-final place.
Draper, who eliminated Hamburg Open winner Andrei Medvedev in the first round but had never previously beaten a top 10 player, defeated Muster at his own game.
"He's probably recognised as one of the toughest players on clay in the world and the scary part about it is that I actually won physically and mentally," said the world number 75.
While the centre court furnace dehydrated a man famed for his fitness, Draper -- familiar with the heat and humidity of his hometown Brisbane in Queensland -- revelled in it.
"I love the heat because I know I can handle it better than most other players," he said.
At times, the Australian even outdid the Austrian's tough guy image, continually shouting at himself and hurling his racket to the ground in anger at unforced errors.
Draper recovered from 2-4 down and 4-5 on the Muster serve to take the first set into a tiebreak which he dominated with breathtaking backhand winners.
The Australian broke to lead 2-0 in the second before the heat got to him. "I had a letdown," he said, "the first set was the toughest I've ever played.
In a topsy-turvy set, both men held breakpoints until Muster levelled the match on his second set point.
In a tight final set Muster started to struggle while Draper continued to chase down every ball. At 5-5 the Austrian ceded his serve on a double fault and Draper served out the match.
"It's funny what a week can do," said Draper. "If you'd seen me last week, you'd have thought, God, who's this guy."
Defeat means Muster has now failed to progress beyond the third round at any of his four tournaments on clay this season -- a worrying trend ahead of the French Open in Paris.
Jim Courier, conqueror of Sampras in the first round and twice a winner here, in 1992 and 1993, reached the third round with a straight sets win over Spanish qualifier Albert Portas.
But Tuesday's other giantkiller Hernan Gumy, who knocked out Chang, was brought back to earth by another unseeded former champion Sergi Bruguera of Spain 6-1 6-4.

Number 12 seed Becker, making light of his lack of match practice -- nine matches all season - said he did not think he could play any better on clay after brushing off Pioline to set up a third-round clash with Goran Ivanesevic.
The German served four consecutive aces. Asked when he last peformed the feat, he replied: "I was actually thinking that in the match and I don't remember."
